title: Wine remains Australia’s most purchased category as alcohol consumption moderates
summary:
New research shows that wine endures as “the most widely purchased category” in Australia at 55%, followed by spirits at 46% and beer at 44%. The new ‘What’s Driving Australia’s Alcohol Shopper: Consumption, Channels, Promotions and Occasions’ report from Vypr and Shop! ANZ found that 41% of Australians are drinking less than a year ago or have stopped altogether, while only 6% are drinking more. Notably, “wine becomes more prominent through middle age, reaching 71% among 35–44s and 63% among 45–54s”. However, among 18–24-year-olds, beer reaches 64% and RTDs 46%, while spirits reach 68% among 25–34s. Additionally, the report emphasises that Australia’s liquor market is shifting from volume to value, with shoppers spending more per bottle-shop visit even as alcohol consumption moderates.

content:
New research shows that wine endures as “the most widely purchased category” in Australia at 55%, followed by spirits at 46% and beer at 44%.

The new ‘What’s Driving Australia’s Alcohol Shopper: Consumption, Channels, Promotions and Occasions’ report from Vypr and Shop! ANZ found that 41% of Australians are drinking less than a year ago or have stopped altogether, while only 6% are drinking more.

Notably, “wine becomes more prominent through middle age, reaching 71% among 35–44s and 63% among 45–54s”.

However, among 18–24-year-olds, beer reaches 64% and RTDs 46%, while spirits reach 68% among 25–34s.

Additionally, the report emphasises that Australia’s liquor market is shifting from volume to value, with shoppers spending more per bottle-shop visit even as alcohol consumption moderates.

48% now typically spend more than $40 per liquor-store shop, up from around 23% a year ago. Among 25–34-year-olds, 64% typically spend above $40.

“With many Australians continuing to cut back on alcohol, brands and retailers will need to compete harder for a share of spending on the occasions when people do choose to drink,” said Sam Gilding, chief revenue officer at Vypr.

“That means understanding who the shopper is, where they want to buy and what combination of product, format and price makes that purchase feel worthwhile.”

A few key findings from the report are as follows:

‘Category strategies need to become more targeted’

The report claims that the differences in wine purchase popularity across age groups points to “a need for more targeted ranging, channel and activation strategies rather than a single approach to all shoppers”.

It emphasises that the holiday season creates another growth opportunity, with Christmas Day influencing alcohol purchases for 52% of consumers, while Christmas parties and gifting influence 47% each and New Year’s Eve 46%.

Gilding added that it’s vital for brands and retailers to understand who they’re targeting and reflect those preferences in their range and promotions.

“Those differences matter as we head into Christmas. Someone buying a gift may be looking for something quite different from someone choosing drinks for a party. Helping shoppers find the right option for their occasion and budget will be important in winning that purchase.”

‘Younger shoppers are reshaping the path to purchase’

Physical retail “remains dominant, with 74% primarily buying alcohol in-store, but younger shoppers are increasingly omnichannel”.

Only 55% of 18–24-year-olds and 58% of 25–34-year-olds primarily shop in-store, while 37% of 25–34s combine physical and online purchasing. The findings suggest digital shopping is complementing rather than replacing physical retail, increasing the need for consistent ranging, pricing and promotion across channels.

‘Price still wins attention, but value is broadening’

Price remains the strongest influence at the point of purchase. Special price tickets are noticed by 63% of shoppers and influence product choice for 61%.

Loyalty points now influence 44% of shoppers, up from 28% for loyalty or member offers a year ago, while bonus packs influence 36% and cashback 33%.

“Price remains incredibly effective at stopping the shopper, but value is becoming broader than on-sale prices alone,” said Carla Bridge, general manager at Shop! ANZ.

“Loyalty, added product, sampling and staff advocacy on a product can all help move the consumer into purchase. The strongest activations will give shoppers a reason to stop and try.”

title: SA wine professionals to head overseas for knowledge exchange program
summary:
Four South Australian wine industry representatives have been selected to travel to some of the world’s most renowned wine regions to “connect with international experts and explore new ideas and innovations”. The South Australian Government explained that ‘The Great Wine Capitals Outbound Knowledge Exchange Bursary Program’ enables wine industry professionals, academics and researchers to visit world-renowned wine regions within the Great Wine Capitals Global Network, exchange knowledge with international peers and bring valuable insights back to South Australia. The state government said the program offers valuable professional development opportunities that strengthen skills, encourage knowledge exchange and enable insights to benefit the state’s wine sector and support its resilience. “South Australia is home to many of the world’s very best premium wine regions, so it’s important to stay ahead of the game by investing in the professionals who keep our state’s wine sector in the global spotlight,” said Clare Scriven, Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development.

content:
Top row LTR: Jodie Armstrong and Luke Willis. Bottom row LTR: Nicole Brasier and Susi Whiting. Images supplied

Four South Australian wine industry representatives have been selected to travel to some of the world’s most renowned wine regions to “connect with international experts and explore new ideas and innovations”.

The South Australian Government explained that ‘The Great Wine Capitals Outbound Knowledge Exchange Bursary Program’ enables wine industry professionals, academics and researchers to visit world-renowned wine regions within the Great Wine Capitals Global Network, exchange knowledge with international peers and bring valuable insights back to South Australia.

The 2026–27 Outbound Knowledge Exchange Bursary Program recipients are:

  • Jodie Armstrong — McLaren Vale Grape Wine and Tourism Association, McLaren Vale (to visit Valparaiso-Casablanca Valley, Chile)
  • Nicole Brasier — Bleasdale Vineyards, Langhorne Creek (to visit Porto, Portugal)
  • Susi Whiting — Adelaide University, Adelaide (to visit Verona, Italy)
  • Luke Willis — Two Hands Wines, Barossa Valley (to visit Mendoza, Argentina)

Jodie Armstrong will explore how to use regenerative soil health practices, along with water and climate knowledge, to build healthier, more resilient vineyards.

Nicole Brasier will explore how the historic fortified wine region has adapted to change while maintaining its traditions in a modern industry, remaining relevant and appealing to premium visitors.

Susi Whiting will learn how vineyards are being used for practical teaching, research and industry engagement, including the region’s approaches to sustainability and adapting to climate change.

Luke Willis will explore how the region uses environmental sustainability practices and vineyard biodiversity to attract high-value international visitors and turn them into long-term direct-to-consumer customers and advocates.

The state government said the program offers valuable professional development opportunities that strengthen skills, encourage knowledge exchange and enable insights to benefit the state’s wine sector and support its resilience.

“South Australia is home to many of the world’s very best premium wine regions, so it’s important to stay ahead of the game by investing in the professionals who keep our state’s wine sector in the global spotlight,” said Clare Scriven, Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development.

“From sustainability and climate adaptation, to enhancing consumer experiences and engagement, each bursary recipient will explore practical innovations that can help to strengthen resilience and competitiveness in our wine sector.

“I congratulate Jodie, Nicole, Susi and Luke on being selected for bursaries through this program and I look forward to seeing how their experiences benefit the South Australian wine industry.”

Each bursary is valued at $6,000, supporting travel to one or more Great Wine Capitals between October 2026 and March 2027. During their travels, recipients will engage with academic, regional and industry experts, exchanging insights and gaining knowledge about global practices, sustainability and innovation in viticulture, winemaking, tourism and research.

Wine Grape Council of South Australia (WGCSA) CEO Lisa Bennier said the organisation is pleased to support a bursary and the opportunities it will provide for professional development.

“Supporting initiatives that build capability and encourage people to bring new knowledge and perspectives back to our industry is an important investment in its future,” Bennier said.

Australian Wine Industry Technical Conference chair Mark Krstic said they are excited to support Jodie Armstrong’s selection for a bursary.

title: Yarra Valley winery makes its US debut on Wall Street
summary:
Levantine Hill is expanding into the US, marking a “major milestone” for the family-owned Yarra Valley estate. Ranked number two in The Real Review’s Top Wineries of Australia 2026, the winery made its USA debut as the official wine partner of the American Australian Association’s 2026 New York Benefit Dinner. On Thursday 5 November, the estate’s wines “were served to hundreds of leaders from business, government and diplomacy at the Manhattan gala, which counted many Fortune 500 companies among its sponsors”. The winery explained that each guest was given a take home bottle of Levantine Hill’s 2019 Samantha’s Paddock Mélange Traditionnel, its flagship Cabernet blend.

The post Yarra Valley winery makes its US debut on Wall Street appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Paul Bridgeman and Melissa Jreissati. Image supplied

Levantine Hill is expanding into the US, marking a “major milestone” for the family-owned Yarra Valley estate.

Ranked number two in The Real Review’s Top Wineries of Australia 2026, the winery made its USA debut as the official wine partner of the American Australian Association’s 2026 New York Benefit Dinner.

On Thursday 5 November, the estate’s wines “were served to hundreds of leaders from business, government and diplomacy at the Manhattan gala, which counted many Fortune 500 companies among its sponsors”.

The winery explained that each guest was given a take home bottle of Levantine Hill’s 2019 Samantha’s Paddock Mélange Traditionnel, its flagship Cabernet blend.

“Levantine Hill was founded on the belief that Australian wines can stand alongside the finest in the world,” said chief winemaker Paul Bridgeman.

“Now we have an opportunity to bring that belief to the table in New York. We want American wine lovers to taste the character of our Yarra Valley vineyards and discover just how compelling cool climate Australian fine wine can be.”

Back in the Yarra Valley, the Jreissati family is preparing to open a 33-suite luxury hotel at Levantine Hill.

“We want someone to discover Levantine Hill over a glass of wine in New York, Las Vegas, Singapore or Seoul, then come to the Yarra Valley and experience the place it comes from,” said marketing director Melissa Jreissati.

“Bringing our wines to the United States builds on Levantine Hill’s ambition to be an international beacon for Australian fine wine and bring our wines to more tables around the world. When our Yarra Valley hotel opens, we’ll be able to welcome more international guests to our very own Yarra Valley table.”

title: Marnong Estate unveils its first-ever Reserve Chardonnay
summary:
Marnong Estate has unveiled its first-ever Reserve Chardonnay as a part its new collection of cool-climate expressions from the estate's Sunbury vineyards. The 2024 Reserve Chardonnay leads the new range which features the 2025 Single Vineyard Chardonnay and 2025 Estate Chardonnay, offering “distinct interpretations of the variety, showcasing the different expressions of fruit, site and winemaking across the estate”. The spring collection also introduces the 2026 Estate Sangiovese Rosé, which marks the first vintage of Marnong Estate’s Sangiovese fruit crafted specifically for rosé.

The post Marnong Estate unveils its first-ever Reserve Chardonnay appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The new wine range features its first-ever Reserve Chardonnay. Image supplied

Marnong Estate has unveiled its first-ever Reserve Chardonnay as a part its new collection of cool-climate expressions from the estate’s Sunbury vineyards.

The 2024 Reserve Chardonnay leads the new range which features the 2025 Single Vineyard Chardonnay and 2025 Estate Chardonnay, offering “distinct interpretations of the variety, showcasing the different expressions of fruit, site and winemaking across the estate”.

The spring collection also introduces the 2026 Estate Sangiovese Rosé, which marks the first vintage of Marnong Estate’s Sangiovese fruit crafted specifically for rosé.

“Chardonnay is such an important part of what we’re doing at Marnong Estate, and the release of our first Reserve Chardonnay is an exciting milestone for the wine program,” said Alex Beckett, Marnong Estate director of wine.

“The Reserve is a wine we only make when we believe the vintage and the fruit have the quality to warrant that level of selection. Alongside the Single Vineyard and Estate Chardonnays, it also gives us the opportunity to show the different expressions of the same variety across our vineyards.

“The Sangiovese Rosé brings something a little different again, with its vibrant fruit, savoury character and Italian varietal heritage making it particularly well suited to spring and summer entertaining.”

Marnong Estate’s new spring releases are available nationally through independent merchants, at the Marnong Estate cellar door and online via the winery’s website.

The post Charlotte Newton awarded Dux of the 2026 Len Evans Tutorial appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Charlotte Newton has been awarded the Dux prize for 2026. Image supplied

Charlotte Newton, owner and winemaker at Cha Cha Wines in Western Australia, has been awarded the Basil Sellers Prize for Dux of the 2026 Len Evans Tutorial.

Newton, along with 11 other Australian wine professionals, took part in the 24th Tutorial held at Spicer’s Guesthouse in the Hunter Valley from 2 to 6 November. As Dux, Charlotte receives $10,000 to further her global wine education.

Originally from New Zealand, Newton studied winemaking at Christchurch’s Lincoln University before building her career in Australia and overseas. Her 25-year career has spanned winemaking, viticulture, wine education and sensory evaluation, with 15 years as a WSET educator.

“I am incredibly proud and honoured to have been awarded Dux of the 2026 Len Evans Tutorial,” Newton said.

“To have been accepted into the Tutorial was a privilege in itself, and the experience exceeded all expectations. I had the opportunity to taste some of the most exceptional wines of my life, form lasting friendships and learn alongside an inspiring group of wine professionals.

“I will cherish these memories for many years to come and look forward to continuing to share my passion for fine wine through wine education and winemaking. Finally, my sincere thanks to the late Len Evans for his vision and to his daughter Sally Evans for continuing his remarkable legacy.”

Selected from a record 193 applications, the 12 scholars represented some of Australia’s most promising wine talent, spanning winemakers, media and trade professionals. Over an intensive week, they learnt from an exceptional line-up of world-class tutors, gaining the knowledge, skills and experience to help shape the future of Australian wine. The programme aims to strengthen the next generation of wine professionals and wine show judges.

“As we see each year via the rigorous selection process, performance remained tight across the cohort for the majority of the week and Charlotte was not only consistent, [but] she [also] spoke to the wines with a deep conviction,” said Sarah Crowe, LET tutor and deputy chair.

“In the final few sessions, this year’s Dux did not falter and was the top performer in the written exercise as well as the final tasting of Domaine de la Romanee-Conti.”

The scholars undertook masterclasses from Australia and further afield, including Henschke, led by Prue and Stephen Henschke, Barolo and Barbaresco with the UK’s David Gleave MW, Burgundy, Prestige Champagne, Hunter Valley Semillon with a vertical of Tyrrell’s Vat 1 with Chris Tyrrell and concluding with Friday’s showcase of Domaine de la Romanee-Conti.

A core component of the programme is the five judging workshops, each featuring 30 wines served blind. These judging sessions focus on grape varieties and styles relevant to the Australian wine industry, this year covering Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon blends, Pinot Noir, Riesling and Chardonnay.

Highlights this year included:

Riesling

  • 2019 Dr Loosen Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett
  • 2018 Castle Rock Estate
  • 2017 Jim Barry The Florita

Chardonnay

  • 2024 Tolpuddle Vineyard
  • 2020 Domaine Caroline Morey Les Champs Gain 1er Cru
  • 2019 Oakridge 864 Funder & Diamond Drive Block

Cabernet

  • 2020 Deep Woods Estate Reserve
  • 2020 Chateau Haut-Brion
  • 2021 Yalumba The Menzies

Shiraz

  • 2024 Yarra Yering Underhill
  • 2022 Domaine Rene Rostang Cote Rotie La Landonne
  • 2022 Koomilya Shiraz

Pinot Noir

  • 2025 Bream Creek
  • 2022 Domaine Dujac Clos Saint-Denis Grand Cru
  • 2025 Yabby Lake Single Vineyard

The tradition of formal dinners continued each evening, starting with a deep dive into the ‘History and Heritage of Australia Wine’ lead by Andrew Caillard MW. A series of aged and rare wine flights were presented, “offering scholars a unique opportunity to experience exceptional vintages that may not be readily available elsewhere”.

“Another great year for the LET, with enthusiasm for the tutorial reaching record levels. Huge thanks to all who helped create a life-changing experience for our 2026 scholars. Whilst sharing, tasting and talking about wine quality is a key focus, the tutorial has also become a vital hub for sharing Australia’s rich wine history. My father achieved many things in his life, but the tutorial is perhaps his most meaningful legacy,” said chair Sally Evans.

The 2026 Scholars were:

  • Alexandra Alavoine (winemaker, Treasury Wine Estates, SA)
  • Jessica Clark (wine science tutor, University of Melbourne; sales, marketing & winemaking, Dexter Wines, VIC)
  • Jacopo Dalli Cani (chief winemaker, McHenry Hohnen Vintners, WA)
  • Alice Davidson (owner & winemaker, Aunt Alice Wines, TAS)
  • Brendan Hawker (senior winemaker, Yering Station, VIC)
  • Annabel Holland (senior winemaker, First Creek Wines, NSW)
  • Jacinta Jenkins (winemaker, Pocket Gully, SA)
  • Tom Kline (wine writer & critic, VIC)
  • Mike Latham (senior winemaker, Giant Steps Wine, VIC)
  • Livia Maiorana (co-owner & winemaker, South by South West Wines, WA)
  • Charlotte Newton (owner and winemaker, Cha Cha Wines; WSET Educator, WA)
  • Emma Shaw (general manager & winemaker, Collector Wines, NSW)

title: Orlando 2025 Cellar 13 Grenache wins James Halliday Grenache Challenge
summary:
The Orlando 2025 Cellar 13 Grenache has received the highest accolade at the 10th annual James Halliday Grenache Challenge, judged in McLaren Vale on 20th October 2026. The judges assessed 169 single-varietal Grenache wines from around Australia, “celebrating the growing strength and incredible diversity of the variety”. “The Orlando Cellar 13 Grenache is a worthy winner of the 2026 James Halliday Grenache Challenge, and a wine the panel kept returning to through the final rounds,” said chair of judges Tony Barlow.

The post Orlando 2025 Cellar 13 Grenache wins James Halliday Grenache Challenge appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Orlando chief winemaker Paul Gobell said the winery is thrilled to have won. Image supplied

The Orlando 2025 Cellar 13 Grenache has received the highest accolade at the 10th annual James Halliday Grenache Challenge, judged in McLaren Vale on 20th October 2026.

The judges assessed 169 single-varietal Grenache wines from around Australia, “celebrating the growing strength and incredible diversity of the variety”.

“The Orlando Cellar 13 Grenache is a worthy winner of the 2026 James Halliday Grenache Challenge, and a wine the panel kept returning to through the final rounds,” said chair of judges Tony Barlow.

“It’s a great example of modern Australian grenache. Incredibly bright colour with density, lifted varietal aromatics with skilful winemaking bringing complexity and a palate that is both generous and detailed. An impressively rich flavoured style but still bright and lithe is no mean feat.

“The margin in the final taste off between six Grenaches from 3 different regions was very close; but the elements listed above won the judges over. Congratulations to the winner on a superb wine.”

Orlando chief winemaker Paul Gobell said they are “absolutely thrilled” to win the top accolade among an impressive field of wines from across the country.

“Grenache is an exciting variety for the Barossa, and we’ve worked hard to capture its vibrant fruit, depth and elegance in this wine. It’s fantastic recognition for Orlando and a credit to the passion and dedication of our vineyard and winemaking teams.”

Barlow strongly encouraged Grenache producers and lovers to seek out the top wines – Orlando 2025 Cellar 13 Grenache, Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache and S.C. Pannell 2024 Little Branch Grenache – to appreciate Australia’s on-going Grenache evolution.

The judges were impressed by the overall quality and diversity of styles on show, “from bright, perfumed, wines through to more structured, savoury examples with real depth and tannin length”.

“The best wines showed brightness, fresh fruit spectrums, lifted aromatics, fine but present tannins, and restraint with regard to oak use and impact. These are wines that speak clearly of their site and vintage,” said the judging panel.

Proudly hosted by the McLaren Vale Wine Region each October, the James Halliday Grenache Challenge benchmarks Grenache wines from across Australia. The organisers said it encourages an honest gauge of Australia’s Grenache winemaking form, tracking styles and movements developing across the industry.

title: Melbourne Royal appoints Dan Sims as chair of Wine Awards Committee
summary:
Melbourne Royal has appointed respected wine industry figure Dan Sims, chair of Wine Victoria, as chair of the Melbourne Royal Wine Awards Committee, bringing “extensive industry experience, leadership and a deep commitment to the continued success of one of Australia’s most prestigious wine competitions”. Comprising of representatives from across the Australian wine industry, the Melbourne Royal Wine Awards Committee “plays a vital role in overseeing and shaping the program”. Working closely with Melbourne Royal, the committee “helps ensure the awards remain relevant to the evolving needs of the industry while guiding the competition's future direction”.

The post Melbourne Royal appoints Dan Sims as chair of Wine Awards Committee appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Dan Sims, chair of Wine Victoria, has been appointed as chair of the Melbourne Royal Wine Awards Committee. Image supplied

Melbourne Royal has appointed respected wine industry figure Dan Sims, chair of Wine Victoria, as chair of the Melbourne Royal Wine Awards Committee, bringing “extensive industry experience, leadership and a deep commitment to the continued success of one of Australia’s most prestigious wine competitions”.

Comprising of representatives from across the Australian wine industry, the Melbourne Royal Wine Awards Committee “plays a vital role in overseeing and shaping the program”. Working closely with Melbourne Royal, the committee “helps ensure the awards remain relevant to the evolving needs of the industry while guiding the competition’s future direction”.

As chair, the Melbourne Royal said Sims will lead some of Australia’s most highly regarded wine professionals, drawing on his extensive industry network and passion for Australian wine to support the continued growth and standing of the awards.

The organisation said his appointment reflects its ongoing commitment to industry engagement, innovation and excellence, while strengthening the awards’ position as a benchmark for Australian winemaking achievement.

“We’re delighted to welcome Dan as Chair of the Melbourne Royal Wine Awards Committee,” said Kirrily Waldhorn, Melbourne Royal senior manager food & beverage awards.

“His depth of experience, strong industry relationships and genuine passion for Australian wine make him an excellent addition to the leadership of the awards. The committee plays an important role in ensuring the competition continues to evolve alongside the industry, and Dan’s insight and perspective will be invaluable as we look to its future.”

Sims will co-present this year’s awards alongside Waldhorn at the upcoming Trophy Awards Presentation.

Dan Sims said it is a real privilege to take on the role of chair “at such an important time for the Australian wine industry”.

“The Melbourne Royal Wine Awards have a long-standing reputation for recognising and championing excellence, and I’m looking forward to working alongside the committee and Melbourne Royal to ensure they continue to deliver meaningful value to the greater wine community.

“My first opportunity to step into the role was to catch up with this year’s judging panel and see first-hand not only the calibre of wines being assessed, but the expertise and consideration of the judges. I’m looking forward to sharing in the celebration of this year’s results and co-presenting the awards with Kirrily.”

title: Calabria Family launches 200ml Bélena bottles
summary:
As Australian wine preferences shift and drinking occasions continue to evolve, the Calabria Family is looking beyond the traditional 750ml bottle with its new 200ml Bélena minis. The new format is across the brand’s most popular styles, including Pinot Grigio, Moscato and Rosé. It will arrive in stores from January 2027 and “demonstrates the family’s broader approach to innovation and challenging traditional wine conventions”. “There’s no question it’s a challenging time for the Australian wine industry, which makes innovation and staying relevant to today’s consumers more important than ever,” said Andrew Calabria, sales and marketing director at Calabria Family Wine Group.

The post Calabria Family launches 200ml Bélena bottles appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The launch of the minis is in response to changing drinking occasions and preferences, the winery explained. Image supplied

As Australian wine preferences shift and drinking occasions continue to evolve, the Calabria Family is looking beyond the traditional 750ml bottle with its new 200ml Bélena minis.

The new format is across the brand’s most popular styles, including Pinot Grigio, Moscato and Rosé. It will arrive in stores from January 2027 and “demonstrates the family’s broader approach to innovation and challenging traditional wine conventions”.

“There’s no question it’s a challenging time for the Australian wine industry, which makes innovation and staying relevant to today’s consumers more important than ever,” said Andrew Calabria, sales and marketing director at Calabria Family Wine Group.

“Bélena has always done things a little differently, and the minis are a natural extension of that. They give consumers more choice in how and when they enjoy wine, while opening up new occasions for the category.”

The smaller format launch comes as Bélena sees domestic sales growing 20% despite overall category decline. Since launching in 2021, Calabria said the brand has “established leading positions across key varietals, including #1 Pinot Grigio and Montepulciano in the $15+ segment”.

“Wine has traditionally been built around established formats and occasions, but there is an opportunity to think more broadly about where it fits,” Calabria said.

“For us, innovation isn’t about changing wine for the sake of it. It’s about understanding how people are living and creating products and experiences that give them more choice. Bélena gives us the freedom to explore that thinking.”

The Bélena minis will be distributed nationally by the House of Fine Wine network.

title: Brendan Carter of Bottleshock named 2026 Wine Communicator of the Year
summary:
Last night, Brendan Carter from Bottleshock was named the 2026 Wine Communicator of the Year by Wine Communicators of Australia (WCA). The announcement was the culmination of the celebrations at WCA’s sold out annual Awards Night in Sydney, with Brendan accepting his award from WCA National Chair, Lynda Schenk. "The Wine Communicator Awards are a highlight of the year for our community,” said Schenk. “From digital campaigns and events, to journalism, education, research, hospitality and advocacy, the awards celebrate the individuals and organisations helping connect people with wine through compelling stories, fresh ideas and meaningful conversations. The Wine Communicator of the Year, Brendan Carter, demonstrates an exceptional ability to engage consumers through his Bottleshock.TV and The Big Blind League wine tasting competition while also challenging us all to act differently in how we talk about wine. His fresh thinking, willingness to challenge convention, and commitment to building stronger connections between wine and consumers make him a truly deserving recipient of this honour.”

content:
The 2026 award winners at The Wine Communicator Awards, holding Brendan Carter. Image supplied

Last night, Brendan Carter from Bottleshock was named the 2026 Wine Communicator of the Year by Wine Communicators of Australia (WCA).

The announcement was the culmination of the celebrations at WCA’s sold out annual Awards Night in Sydney, with Brendan accepting his award from WCA National Chair, Lynda Schenk.

“The Wine Communicator Awards are a highlight of the year for our community,” said Schenk.

“From digital campaigns and events, to journalism, education, research, hospitality and advocacy, the awards celebrate the individuals and organisations helping connect people with wine through compelling stories, fresh ideas and meaningful conversations.

“The Wine Communicator of the Year, Brendan Carter, demonstrates an exceptional ability to engage consumers through his Bottleshock.TV and The Big Blind League wine tasting competition while also challenging us all to act differently in how we talk about wine. His fresh thinking, willingness to challenge convention, and commitment to building stronger connections between wine and consumers make him a truly deserving recipient of this honour.”

Upon being named the winner, Carter said commanding people’s attention is a privilege.

“The most important thing when it comes to building audiences is trust and authenticity and that is where Australia has a unique opportunity. Very few accents click in people’s minds globally as the Australian one. The ability to command attention is becoming scarcer but if we can establish Australian accents globally as the authority on wine now, we might just be okay,” he said.

The annual Wine Communicator Awards recognise outstanding excellence in wine communication in all its forms.

33 experienced and respected industry professionals judged entries across 13 different categories. The judges were hugely impressed with the calibre of creativity, passion and skill shown across a wide range of communication channels.

Toasts were also made to the 13 category winners with trophy-winning wines from this year’s Sydney Royal Wine Awards.

content:
LTR: Tom Bartholomaeus and Nigel Blieschke of Torbreck Vintners

By Kyra Trussell

Last Thursday, a well-attended workshop discussing and demonstrating reworking old vine Grenache was held in the Barossa Valley.

Hosted by The Barossa Viticulture Technical Group (BVTG) and led by technical viticulturist Tom Bartholomaeus as well as chief viticulturist Nigel Blieschke of Torbreck Vintners, the morning led attendees through three blocks of Grenache vines.

The first block had been successfully reworked in 2020 with an approximate 95% strike rate. Shoot thinning had been performed at this site to manage vine density, prevent clumping and improve airflow.

“If you look at the shadow of these vines, there’s dappled light. That’s a really good indicator of the quality of Grenache,” Blieschke said of the first block.

The second block was reworked two years later in 2022 with a 75% strike rate, which Bartholomaeus said was a disappointing result.

He went on to explain that, compared to the first block, the second site was around 1.3 tonne to the hectare lower in yields.

“We just struggled to get things growing, so a lot of the cordons are a bit shorter. We’re still trying to extend them in places, just with regard to how we do that in a in a soft pruning practice.

“We’ll always kind of go halfway with putting a new cordon down, leave a shoot from a downward facing bud, and we’ll extend that in the second year to ensure that we get really good growth on our shoots as we go.

“That’s been a far lengthier process in here, and the depth is something that’s held us back as well. So, we thought that we could speed up the process, and you’ll see that the shoot length in here probably isn’t as good either — that’s because we find that our trunks are just a little bit weaker too. We just got a little bit too excited,” Bartholomaeus reflected.

Blieschke emphasised to the attendees that there was an important lesson to learn from the second block.

“None of this is short-term, you’ve got to be prepared to do the work over time…slow and steady rather than flat out, take your time,” he urged.

The third block was a yet to be reworked project for 2026 which Bartholomaeus described as “a combination of the lessons that we’ve learned in other bits and pieces that we’ve done”.

“We want to give it a year or two to see if we can push some material down low to begin with. I think [with] vine number two,” he gestured to the second vine in the row, “we’ve got success in that we had a water shoot that was growing down low and were able to cut off the top end of the vine, and that’s good to go — that’s a vine that we’ll consider starting the spur pruning journey on next year, but we’ve also left material.”

“Do you prioritise future or fruit? That’s the question,” Blieschke added.

“A lot of knowledge from Europe would say if you’re going for future, don’t go for fruit. This one is for the future. When we are pruning those vines, our pruners are thinking about if they’re all growing together, they’re looking to not grow together,” he explained to the audience.

Guests were given the opportunity to inspect multiple soil pits across the three vineyards, which were created to showcase what viticulturists should look for in healthy Grenache root system growths and to discuss the irrigation requirements of the vines.

A standout piece of advice from the event was the benefits Torbreck had found from using the same four pruners for 10 years.

Bartholomaeus told of how they save time and effort not having to reteach the intricacies of each vineyard by bringing back a team who knows the blocks well.

Longevity was an overarching theme at the workshop, with the two viticulturists demonstrating how they will rework the third vineyard with pruning and a saw to prioritise the future health of the vines.

The workshop ended with SARDI research scientist Tarita Furlan presenting the latest research on preventing and managing Eutypa.
